stem: A scan produces a list of missing patches but does not attempt to break in. To determine whether those weaknesses can actually be exploited, what is MOST appropriate next?

options.text: A penetration test that actively attempts to exploit the weaknesses
options.rationale: A pen test exploits identified weaknesses to demonstrate real-world impact, going beyond the vulnerability assessment's cataloging.
Re-scanning re-lists weaknesses but still does not test exploitability.
Discarding results abandons the findings rather than validating exploitability.
Ignoring known weaknesses leaves them unaddressed and unvalidated.

stem: Before a penetration test begins, what MUST happen FIRST?

options.text: Obtain written authorization and agree on rules of engagement/scope
options.rationale: Written authorization and defined rules of engagement are mandatory before testing; testing without them can be illegal.

options.text: Immediately start exploiting systems to save time
options.rationale: Exploiting systems without authorization is unauthorized access and potentially illegal.
Publicizing vulnerabilities is harmful and not a pre-test step.

options.text: Disable the target's logging without permission
options.rationale: Tampering with the target without authorization is improper and out of scope.

stem: A test in which the tester is given full knowledge including source code and architecture is MOST accurately which type, and what is its main advantage?

options.text: White box testing — the most thorough coverage due to full knowledge
options.rationale: White box testing leverages complete knowledge/source access to achieve the most thorough coverage of the target.

options.text: Black box testing — no knowledge, most thorough
options.rationale: Black box has no prior knowledge and is less thorough than white box, not more.
Gray box has partial, not full, knowledge.

options.text: Blind testing that ignores the code
options.rationale: White box specifically uses the code; ignoring it contradicts the definition.

stem: To most realistically simulate an external attacker with no inside information, which testing approach is BEST?

options.rationale: Black box testing gives the tester no prior knowledge, closely simulating an outside attacker's starting position.

options.text: White box testing with full source access
options.rationale: Full knowledge does not simulate an external attacker with no information.
Not testing provides no simulation at all.

options.text: Giving the tester admin credentials up front
options.rationale: Providing credentials contradicts the no-knowledge external-attacker simulation.

stem: An organization wants to know whether its SOC can detect and respond to a stealthy, realistic intrusion over time. Which exercise is MOST appropriate?

options.text: A red team exercise (adversary simulation testing detection and response)
options.rationale: Red teaming stealthily emulates a real adversary to test the organization's detection and response, not just vulnerability presence.
A scan lists weaknesses but does not evaluate detection/response over time.
Style review checks code formatting, unrelated to testing SOC response.
Restore testing validates recovery, not intrusion detection/response.

stem: To find input-handling flaws by sending malformed and unexpected data to an application, which technique is BEST?

options.rationale: Fuzzing feeds malformed/random input to trigger crashes and reveal input-handling vulnerabilities.
Surveys gather opinions, not input-handling defects.
Backup review is unrelated to input-handling testing.
Physical audits do not exercise application input handling.

stem: A team runs scripted transactions against a web app around the clock to detect availability and performance problems before users do. This technique is MOST accurately called what?

options.rationale: Synthetic transactions are scripted, simulated user actions run continuously to monitor availability/performance proactively.
Pen testing exploits weaknesses; it is not scripted availability monitoring.
Fuzzing sends malformed input to find crashes, not to monitor availability with valid transactions.
Static analysis inspects source code, not live transaction availability.

stem: To find security defects in source code without executing the program, which technique is BEST?

options.rationale: Static analysis/code review inspects source code without running it, catching defects early.

options.text: Running the app and fuzzing only
options.rationale: Fuzzing tests the running app; it does not inspect source code statically.
Ping tests connectivity, not source-code defects.
Physical audits do not examine source code.

stem: During a pen test, the tester discovers an out-of-scope system that looks vulnerable. What is the MOST appropriate action?

options.text: Do not test it; document it and consult the client to amend scope if desired
options.rationale: Testers must stay within the authorized scope; exploiting out-of-scope systems is unauthorized. The finding is reported and scope can be formally amended.

options.text: Immediately exploit it since it looks vulnerable
options.rationale: Exploiting out-of-scope systems exceeds authorization and may be illegal.

options.text: Delete the system to be safe
options.rationale: Destroying systems is never an appropriate testing action.
Silently ignoring a discovered risk fails to inform the client; it should be documented.

stem: A vulnerability assessment primarily produces which of the following?

options.text: A catalog of identified weaknesses without exploiting them
options.rationale: A vulnerability assessment identifies and lists weaknesses; exploitation is the pen test's role.

options.text: Proof that each weakness was successfully exploited
options.rationale: Demonstrating exploitation is what a penetration test does, not a vulnerability assessment.
Marketing plans are unrelated to vulnerability assessment output.
Backup scheduling is not a vulnerability assessment deliverable.

stem: After authorization is obtained, which pen-test phase generally comes FIRST?

options.rationale: Following planning/authorization, testers gather information (reconnaissance) before scanning and exploitation.
Reporting is the last phase, not the first after authorization.
Post-exploitation occurs after successful exploitation, not first.
Exploitation follows reconnaissance and scanning, not precedes them.

stem: A client gives testers limited internal information to make testing more efficient while retaining some realism. This is MOST accurately which approach?

options.rationale: Gray box provides partial knowledge, balancing external-attacker realism with the efficiency of some inside information.
Black box provides no prior information, which the scenario contradicts.
White box provides full knowledge/source, more than the 'limited' information described.
There is no such standard category; the described partial knowledge is gray box.

stem: A well-meaning employee runs an exploitation tool against company servers without any written approval. What is the MOST accurate concern?

options.text: Unauthorized testing may violate policy and law, even if intentions are good
options.rationale: Exploiting systems without written authorization can breach policy and computer-crime law regardless of intent.

options.text: It automatically makes the systems more secure
options.rationale: Unauthorized testing does not inherently improve security and creates legal risk.

options.text: There is no concern because they are an employee
options.rationale: Employment does not authorize unapproved exploitation of systems.

options.text: It replaces the need for a formal test
options.rationale: Ad hoc unauthorized activity is not a substitute for a scoped, authorized test.

stem: A team wants to test how an application behaves when someone deliberately abuses a feature (e.g., manipulating a price field). Which testing approach is BEST?

options.rationale: Misuse/abuse case testing deliberately exercises how the app handles malicious or unintended use of features.
Surveys measure satisfaction, not adversarial feature abuse.
Restore testing validates recovery, not feature abuse handling.
Physical inspection is unrelated to application misuse testing.

stem: Relying solely on automated vulnerability scanners has which MOST notable limitation?

options.text: They can produce false positives/negatives and miss complex logic flaws that manual testing catches
options.rationale: Automated scanners are efficient but can misreport and miss business-logic or chained vulnerabilities that require human analysis.

options.text: They are always 100% accurate with no errors
options.rationale: Scanners commonly produce false positives and negatives, contradicting this claim.

options.text: They can never find any vulnerabilities
options.rationale: Scanners do find many vulnerabilities; the limitation is coverage of complex flaws, not total inability.
Scanners identify, not automatically fix, vulnerabilities.

stem: Testing a running application from the outside by sending requests and observing responses is MOST accurately which approach?

options.rationale: Dynamic testing exercises the running application externally, observing behavior, unlike static source analysis.
Static analysis inspects code without running it, the opposite of dynamic testing.
This is unrelated to application testing.
Physical patrols do not test running applications.

stem: Which element is MOST important to define in the rules of engagement for a penetration test?

options.text: The authorized scope, timing, and constraints of the test
options.rationale: ROE define what may be tested, when, and how, keeping the test authorized and controlled.
Personal preferences are irrelevant to ROE.

options.text: The color of the report cover
options.rationale: Report aesthetics are not a rules-of-engagement concern.
This has no bearing on test scope or constraints.

stem: To achieve both broad coverage and depth on business-logic flaws, what is the BEST testing strategy?

options.text: Combine automated scanning for breadth with manual testing for depth on complex logic
options.rationale: Automation covers many checks quickly while skilled manual testing finds nuanced logic flaws scanners miss — together they maximize coverage and depth.

options.text: Use automated scanning only and skip manual testing
options.rationale: Automation alone misses complex logic flaws.

options.text: Use manual testing only for everything, at any scale
options.rationale: Manual-only testing does not scale for breadth across large environments.
Skipping testing provides no assurance at all.

stem: A team analyzes actual production users' interactions to understand real experience and detect issues. This is MOST accurately called what?

options.text: Real user monitoring (passive monitoring of actual traffic)
options.rationale: Real user monitoring observes genuine user interactions in production, complementing synthetic transactions.
Fuzzing sends malformed input, not observation of real users.
Static analysis inspects code, not live user traffic.
A pen test exploits weaknesses; it is not passive monitoring of real users.

stem: Which of the following is LEAST relevant as a security control testing technique?

options.rationale: Paint color has no role in testing whether security controls work, making it least relevant.
Pen testing is a core control-testing technique.
Vulnerability assessment is a fundamental testing technique.
Code review is a relevant technique for finding source defects.
